sections.title: Part Iv - Directive Principles of State Policy

blocks.text: [Article 36-51]
Salient Features of DPSP
DPSPs are non-justiciable, means that they are not legally enforceable by courts.
The concept is borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
They place positive obligations on the State to promote social and economic justice.
Their objective is to help establish social and economic democracy.
DPSPs reflect the vision of a Welfare State as outlined in the Constitution.
They serve as a measure to assess laws based on their alignment with constitutional ideals.
Novel Features/Resemble the Instrument of Instructions as contained in Gol Act 1935: B. R. Ambedkar
DPSPs have Moral and Political sanctions.
Comments on DPSP: Conscience of Constitution: Granville Austin
Manifesto of aims and aspirations: K. C. Wheare
Cheque payable by the bank at its own convenience: K. T.
Moral Precepts for the authorities of state: B. N. Rau
T. Krishnamachari: Described DPSPs as a "dustbin of sentiments."
L. M. Singhvi: Called them the "life-giving provisions of the Constitution"
Article 36: Definition of State.
Defines the term "State" as it is used in Part IV.
~• The meaning of "State" here is the same as in Article 12 under Fundamental Rights (Part II).
Article 37: Application of the Principles contained in this part.
They are non-justiciable in nature.
They are fundamental to governance.

It is the duty of the state to apply these principles when making laws and policies Article 38: State to secure a social order for the promotion of welfare of the people (a) The State must promote people's welfare by ensuring justice — social, economic, and political.
(b) It should also reduce inequalities in income, status, facilities, and opportunities. (44th Amendment, 1978)

Article 39: Certain principles of policy to be followed by the State The State should work to ensure: 2 ety · L- (a) Livelihood for all citizens D- (b) Fair distribution of resources for the common good.
C- (c) Avoiding concentration of wealth and production.
P- (d) Equal pay for equal work for men and women.
H- (e) Protection of worker's Health and children from exploitation.
C- (f) Proper development opportunities for Children (42nd Amendment, 1976).
Article 39A: Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid _• Directs the State to ensure equal Justice and provide free legal aid to the poor and weaker sections (42nd CA,1976).
Article 40: Establish Village Panchayats for Self Government.

Article 41: Right to Work, Education, and Public Assistance in certain cases Article 42: Just and Humane Working Conditions & Maternity Relief. In K. Umadevi v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2022), the Supreme Court granted maternity benefits for the third child under the Maternity Benefit (Amendment) Act, 2017.

Article 43: Living Wages and Decent Working Conditions Article 43A: Workers' Participation in Management of Industries — The State shall ensure workers' participation in industry management (42nd Amendment, 1976).
Article 43B: Promotion of Cooperative Societies — The State shall promote the formation and democratic management of cooperative societies (97th Amendment, 2011).
Article 44: Uniform Civil Code

Article 45: Provision for Early Childhood Care and Education — 86th Amendment Act, 2002 changed the subject matter of this article and shifted focus to early childhood care and education for children below the age of six years.
Article 46: Promotion of Educational and Economic Interests of SCs, STs, and Weaker Sections Article 47: To prohibit the consumption of intoxicating drinks and drugs which are injurious to health.
Article 48: Organisation of Agriculture and Animal Husbandry — prohibit slaughter of cows, calves, and useful cattle.
Article 48A: Protection of Environment, Forests, and Wildlife — The State shall protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife (42nd Amendment, 1976).

Article 49: Protection of Monuments and National Heritage Article 50: Separation of Judiciary from Executive Article 51: Promotion of International Peace and Security 51(1): Settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
Classification of DPSPs: DPSPs Classified into three Principles
Socialistic principles: Aim for social and economic welfare, focusing on equality and a welfare state.
Gandhian principles: Emphasize on decentralized govern- ance, self-sufficiency, and equitable resource distribution.
Liberal-Intellectual principles: Prioritize individual freedoms and rights, along with promoting a strong, rational state.

Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951): Supreme Court ruled that—
FRs would prevail over DPSP.
Golaknath Case (1967): Parliament cannot revoke/amend FRs.
Aftermath of The Golaknath case:
In response to the Golaknath case, the Parliament enacted 24th amendment which empowered Parliament to amend FRs.
25th Amendment: Inserted Article 31(C)
(i) Laws implementing DPSP under Articles 39(b) and 39(c) cannot be challenged on the grounds of contravention of Article 14 & 19.
(ii) No such law can be questioned in the court.
Keshavananda Bharti Case (1973): A 13 judges bench ruled that
Parliament can amend FRs but cannot disturb the Basic Structure of the Constitution.
The 2nd provision of the Article 31(C) which restricted judicial reviews of laws was declared unconstitutional.
Minerva Mill Case (1980): Indian Constitution is found on the bedrock of balance between FRs and DPSP.

[Article 51 A]
FDs are borrowed from the USSR.
Statutory and non-enforceable / Non-justiciable
Not originally part of the Constitution.
Introduced through the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act (1976)
Applicable only to Indian citizens, not foreigners.
Committee that suggested addition of Fundamental Duties:
Swaran Singh Committee proposed Fundamental Duties in 1976:
Recommended 8 duties. (Prime Minister - Indira Gandhi)
5 duties accepted, 3 duties rejected.
Rejected duties:
Imposing penalties for not observing duties.
Prohibition against challenging penalty laws in courts.
Duty to pay taxes.
On the recommendations of Swaran Singh Committee the 42nd CA of 1976 was made to add 10 FDs in Part IVA & Article 51 A.
The 11th Fundamental Duty [Article 51A(k)] was added later via 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002.
(a) to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem
(b) to cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom
(c) to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integ- rity of India
(d) to defend the country and render national service when called upon to do so

(e) to promote harmony and the spirit of common brother- hood among all the people of India, transcending religious, linguistic and regional or sectional diversities; to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women
(f) to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture
(g) to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures
(h) to develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform
(i) to safeguard public property and to abjure violence
(j) to strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity so that the nation constantly rises to higher levels of endeavour and achievement
(k) duty of a parent or guardian: to provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between the age of six and fourteen years. (Added through 86th CA, 2002)
Justice Verma Committee:
It identified the existence of legal provisions for imple- mentation of Fundamental Duties and teaching school kids about their duties.
Laws Reflecting and Enforcing Fundamental Duties
The Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (1967)
Prevents activities that threaten the sovereignty and integrity of India — Duty (c)
Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act (1971)
Prohibits disrespect to the Constitution, National Flag, and National Anthem. — Duty (a)
Wildlife Protection Act (1972)
Provides legal protection to wild animals and birds. — Duty (g)
Forest Conservation Act (1980)
> Restricts deforestation and conserves forests. — Duty (g)
Representation of the People Act (1951)
—• Regulates elections and upholds democratic processes. — Duty (a)
Indian Penal Code (IPC)
Defines crimes and prescribes punishments, protecting public order and morality. — Duties (i) and (e) (to renounce derogatory practices against women)
Protection of Civil Rights Act (1955)
Eliminates untouchability and promotes equality. —Duty (e)
Fundamental duties are provided for Indian citizens only and not for Foreigners.
According to H. R. Gokhale (then Law Minister), Fundamental Duties were added in 1976 to control anti- national and unconstitutional activities that increased before the 1975 Emergency.
The Fundamental Duties partly resemble the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR).
The Constitution Review Commission (2002) chaired by M. N. Venkatachaliah recommended measures for effective implementation of Fundamental Duties.
